title: Wash your bowl
hookLine: a new monk asks for teaching, Zhaozhou asks if he's eaten, and says: then wash your bowl (Gateless Gate, case 7)

cards: Sign up for the class, join the gym, open the book everyone talks about, and on the first day it's tempting to walk in ready for the big secret. Tell me the thing. The real thing.
The key. Now, a young monk in China, more than a thousand years ago, does exactly that. He's just entered the monastery.
He finds the old master, Zhaozhou, one of the most well-known teachers in the history of Zen, and asks, earnestly: I've just arrived. Please, teach me. And Zhaozhou asks him about breakfast.

teach.b: This one comes from a real book: the Gateless Gate, a collection of forty-eight short Zen cases gathered in China in the twelve hundreds by a monk named Wumen. It's case seven, only a few lines long.
The monk says: I've just entered the monastery. Please teach me.
Zhaozhou asks: have you eaten your rice porridge? The monk says: yes, I have. And Zhaozhou says: then wash your bowl.
The book says the monk understood. No lecture. No secret.

The monk wanted something special, and Zhaozhou pointed him at the dishes. Here's what makes it more than a brush-off. In a Zen monastery, washing your bowl isn't a chore you do before the practice starts.
It is the practice. Eat when you eat. Wash when you wash.
Do the next plain thing completely, with your whole attention, instead of reaching past it for something grander. Zen kept saying this, in many voices.

The Japanese teacher Dogen, who studied in China and came home in 1227, wrote a whole set of instructions for the monastery cook, and treated washing rice and scrubbing pots as seriously as sitting in the meditation hall.
And notice what Zhaozhou didn't say. He didn't call the porridge unimportant, or tell the monk to hurry past breakfast to the real teaching. He sent him back to the bowl he'd just used.
The teaching isn't hidden somewhere else.
It's in your hands, in the warm water, in the bowl. You don't need a mountain or a retreat. A sink and one dish are enough.

how: In Zen monasteries, meals are eaten in silence from a set of nested bowls that each monk cleans at the table, and daily work like cooking and cleaning is treated as part of practice, not a break from it.

practice: If you can, go to a sink now; if not, picture it clearly, and wash one dish slowly, front and back: the temperature of the water, the weight of the dish, the soap sliding.
When your mind runs ahead, and it will, come back to the bowl. Dry it, and put it away.
